book.title: Alcman & the Cosmos of Sparta
book.summary: The Partheneion, or “maiden song,” composed in the seventh century BCE by the SpartanpoetAlcman, is the earliest substantial example of a choral lyric. A provocative reinterpretation of the Partheneion and its broader context, Alcman and the Cosmos of Sparta excavates the poem’s invocations of widespread and long-lived cosmological ideas that cast the universe as perfectly harmonious and invested its workings with an ethical dimension. Moving far beyond standard literary interpretations, Gloria Ferrari uncovers this astral symbolism by approaching the poem from several angles to brilliantly reconstruct the web of ancient drama, music, religion, painting, and material culture in which it is enmeshed. She shows, for example, that by stringing together images of horses, stars, and birds, the poem evokes classical antiquity’s beloved dance of the constellations.

argument.statement: The Partheneion’s invocations draw on long-lived cosmological ideas that portray the cosmos as harmonious and ethically meaningful, which Ferrari reconstructs to link astral symbolism across drama, music, religion, painting, and material culture.

book.rationale: The book primarily explores the historical context and significance of Alcman's choral lyric, situating it within ancient cultural practices, making History the dominant subject while also addressing elements of literary and artistic analysis.
